text: Mirek Dvořák, mechanic, hangar one. Up the mountain, a pass like this opens doors.
A green tiled stove the size of a wardrobe. Marta says it has not gone out since 1911. Neither, I think, has Marta.
Snow, pine forest, and the mountain the locals call the Observatory. Nobody in Zlatá Hora has ever seen a telescope.
A cuckoo clock with a golden rooster instead of a cuckoo. It crows on the hour. Everyone in the village is very tired.
Two pairs of antlers. According to Marta, both stags died of old age, laughing at the local hunters.
Vasko again, hung slightly crooked. I suspect that's the only act of rebellion in the village.
Marta, landlady of the Golden Rooster. Arms like a stevedore, a laugh like a landslide, and a very good memory for who owes her money.
Mirek, asleep with his head on the table and a smile on his face. He's dreaming of aeroplanes, or slivovitz.
A mechanic in greasy overalls, swaying gently in his seat. A pass on a blue ribbon hangs from his pocket: OBSERVATORY ZLATÁ HORA.
He's snoring. I'll let him sleep. He has a long walk up a mountain in the morning.
Friend! Sit! You look like a man who needs a slivovitz. I am a man who needs another one.
You work up at the Observatory?
Shh! There is no Observatory. I look after a big black bird that does not exist. Dr Veselá shouts at me in three languages.
I missed the last bus up. But the bread van goes at five. I will go with the bread. Tomorrow. Maybe.
He's not letting go of that pass while he's awake. And Marta isn't serving him anything more.
I reach, very casually, for the ribbon...
Hands off! This is my pass! Without it I am nothing. With it, I am also nothing, but in a warm hangar.
Four glasses now: three beers and one very strong glass of water.
Three beers, all finished. Mirek has been celebrating something. Possibly Tuesday.
Twelve days, darling. Twelve days you have sat in this inn, watching that mountain.
I've learned a lot. The bread van goes up every afternoon at five. The mechanics come down every night at eight. And Marta makes the best dumplings in Central Europe.
You have also gained two kilos.
Cover. A thin man in a village inn is suspicious.
Control wants photographs of the aircraft. Real ones. So you will take this.
My Minox. I have photographed three ministers, two generals and a bishop with it. None of them were wearing trousers.
I am taking Ilse and the child over the border tonight. The goose stays. Anička says she is your bodyguard now.
Wonderful. My bodyguard is a goose called Colonel.
Be careful, darling. Mothers do not like to lose their best agents. It spoils the Christmas card list.
Harwig! My favourite refrigerator salesman. Twelve days, and you have not sold one refrigerator.
It's a difficult market, Marta. Everybody here already has snow.
What now, refrigerator man?
What goes on up at the Observatory?
Stars, officially. But at night the mountain hums, the cows give no milk, and something black flies over the church without a sound.
Father Tomáš says it is the Devil. I say the Devil would stop for a beer.
Who goes up the mountain?
Soldiers, in trucks, who do not wave. The mechanics, on the bus. And Vlasta's bread van, every day at five. Soldiers do not bake.
Is Mirek all right?
Mirek has had eleven slivovitz. After eleven, I give him water. He has not noticed for three years.
I'll have what he's having.
One "slivovitz". On the house. Do not tell anybody it is water, it is my best seller.
Nothing, thank you, Marta.
Nothing. The only thing you ever buy.
One for the road, Mirek?
Friend! Na zdraví!
Ahh. Strong. Very strong. The strongest one yet...
Out like a light, from a glass of water. The ribbon has slipped out of his pocket.
Mirek Dvořák, mechanic. He won't need it until the morning. Or, at this rate, next Tuesday.
The square. The bakery, the church, and, on the peak above the village, three little lights where no light should be.
The Observatory. A radar dome on the summit, and slits of light in the rock face. Somebody has hollowed out the whole mountain.
The Church of St Wenceslas. The clock is eleven minutes slow. Nobody in Zlatá Hora is in a hurry to get anywhere.
A telephone box. One of the few in Karvonia that works, and one of the very many that is listened to.
Vlasta's bakery. The smell of bread could make a strong man weep. I've been in here every day for twelve days. That explains the two kilos.
Sacks of flour waiting to go in. MOUKA, fifty kilos each.
Any more flour and they'll bake me.
Roll in the flour, in my own coat, in front of the whole village? I need a better reason.
Vlasta, the baker. Seventy years old, flour to the elbows, and able to carry four trays of rolls at once without looking.
Vlasta's bread van. It goes up the mountain every day at five, and the soldiers wave it straight through. Nobody searches the bread.
Oi! Out of my van! That is the soldiers' supper, not a taxi.
Like that? In a coat like a spy in a film? The guards will shoot you, and then they will shoot me.
I've had enough of London for one day.
Yes?
It's me. I'm going up the mountain tonight.
Good. Photographs, Harrow. Nothing else. Don't touch the aircraft, don't bring it home, and for heaven's sake don't get on it.
Your mother sends her love.
My mother is a national treasure and a national security risk. She tells me you have a goose.
The goose has me, sir.
Photographs, Harrow.
Well? In the van, Pepík. The soldiers want their supper.
Put on the smock, and roll in the flour. Pepík is always covered in flour. It is his only talent.
Rohlíky, koláče, bread for the soldiers! Oh, it is you, the refrigerator man. You want another cake? You will not fit in your coat.
Where are you taking all that bread?
Up the mountain, to the Observatory kitchen. Forty loaves, a hundred rolls. My boy Pepík carries the baskets, but Pepík has the mumps. He looks like a hamster.
And my back is seventy years old. The rest of me is sixty.
Let me carry the bread for you. I'm strong, I'm bored, and I work for cake.
You? The guards know Pepík. Pepík is small, white with flour and not very clever. You are big, clean and far too clever.
I can be very stupid. Ask anyone in London.
Hm. Here. Pepík's smock and his cap. Get some flour on you, and keep your mouth shut. Pepík never talks.
How is business?
Very good. The soldiers eat like wolves, and they pay like wolves too. Which is to say, never.
Goodbye, Vlasta.
Buy some bread next time. You look hungry. Also fat.
One smock, one cap, and half a sack of flour. I look like a ghost who works in a bakery.
The Colonel doesn't recognise me. Good sign.
The van will get me past the gate. But once I'm inside, I'll need to open doors. Mirek's pass, back in the inn.
Good boy, Pepík. In the back, with the baskets. And the goose?
She comes with me.
Then she goes in a basket. If she eats one roll, you pay for it.
Nightglass. Black as a hole in the night, all flat facets and knife edges. It doesn't look built. It looks cut.
Something the size of a bus under a green tarpaulin that says DO NOT TOUCH. I have never wanted to touch anything so much.
I'd love to sit in it. Control specifically said not to. Control is a very dull man.
You! Bread boy! Hands off the tarpaulin, or I bake you.
It weighs a ton. Dr Veselá said she would show me. Let her.
A photograph of a tarpaulin. Control would have it framed and fire me.
Too dark. I'd get a black shape on a black background. Mind you, that's all it looks like anyway.
Thirty-six exposures. Every angle. Even its good side, if it has one.
The test lights, blazing. It's like midday in here, if midday were underground and illegal.
The hangar lights: four switches. Three say NORMAL. The red one says TEST: DO NOT USE WITHOUT AUTHORISATION.
They're on. Any brighter and the jet would get a suntan.
Bread boy! What are you doing by the switches? Bread goes to the kitchen!
Clunk, clunk, clunk. Test lights. Now I can see every rivet in the place.
Blueprints, pinned to a board. NIGHTGLASS, No. 7. Somebody has been improving the design. Somebody very good.
A woman in a white coat with a pencil through her hair, glaring at the blueprints as if they had insulted her mother.
Sergeant Hrubý: twenty stone of Karvonian army, guarding the tarpaulin as if it might run off.
Bread boy. Why are you still here? The kitchen is that way.
Sorry, Sergeant. Lost.
Everybody is lost in this mountain. That is the idea.
You are not Mirek. Mirek has a moustache. Also, Mirek is not a bread boy.
Jet fuel. Stencilled NO SMOKING in four languages, and, underneath, in pencil, PLEASE.
An overhead crane with a hook. The tarpaulin is roped to it, ready to be lifted off.
The office can wait. First, the photographs. That's what I'm here for.
A steel door at the foot of the stairs. AUTHORISED STAFF. A slot for a pass beside the handle.
The office can wait. First, the photographs.
Beep, click. Mirek Dvořák, mechanic, is going upstairs.
Vlasta's van will be long gone, and the flight plan is upstairs. No going back yet.
Vlasta's van leaves in an hour, with me or without me. I haven't got what I came for.
Inside the mountain. A cathedral of rock, and in the middle, under a tarpaulin, the thing that everybody is lying about.
You! Bread boy! The kitchen is through the other door. And what is in that basket?
Bread. It's very fresh.
Fresh bread does not honk.
Karvonian bread does. It's the yeast.
...Carry on.
The office is at the top of the stairs. The flight plans are in his safe. He changes the code every week, and every week it is something about himself.
Well? Take your pictures, bread boy. And switch on the test lights, or you will photograph nothing but shadow.
You are not Pepík.
I've had a very difficult year.
Pepík is twelve, he has a hamster called Stalin, and he has never once walked past this aircraft without asking me how fast it goes. You have not asked. So you already know.
Mach one point four. And invisible to radar. You built it?
Dr Hana Veselá. Vasko stole the plans. I made them work. He has my mother in Karvograd, in a flat with a view of the gasworks. Every day I do not build, she loses a window.
Still here?
Get Sergeant Hrubý away from my aircraft, and I will show you what I have built. He is afraid of nothing on earth.
Nothing?
Well. He was once bitten by a swan. He does not talk about it.
A swan. And I have a basket with something very like a swan in it. Only angrier.
Sergeant, the kitchen asked me to give you this basket. Personally.
For me? Bread? Finally, some respect.
A SWAN! It is a swan! Get it away! Not again! NOT AGAIN!
It's a goose, Sergeant. Technically.
In four years I have never seen him move so fast. You must tell me how you train them.
Very well, not-Pepík. You have earned a look.
Nightglass. Number Seven.
Seven?
The plans you stole in Vienna were for Number One, the prototype. It crashed into a lake. This is Number Seven. There are twelve.
Where are the other eleven?
Ask the Colonel. His flight plans are in the safe in his office. But first, your photographs. Use the test lights, the red switch. Nobody authorises anything here anyway.
Nose, tail, intakes, undercarriage. Thirty-six exposures of the most secret aircraft in the world, on a camera that has seen a bishop without his trousers.
Its good side is the left.
It hasn't got a good side. That's the point.
Not-Pepík! Vasko is at the main gate with Captain Kolar and half the army. The main tunnel is full of soldiers.
Is there another way out?
The service tunnel. It runs under the mountain to the runway. Take the tug, the little tractor by the door. It goes like the devil and steers like a pig.
Come with me.
And my mother loses the last window? No. Take your pictures to London. Tell them there are twelve. And tell them the name of the woman who made them fly.
Hana Veselá. I won't forget.
Everyone forgets engineers. Go!
Colonel Vasko's office. Somehow, I knew it would have a red carpet.
A map of Europe with pins in it: Karvograd, Vienna, Prague. And a dotted red line to Istanbul, circled twice. Vasko is going on holiday.
Another portrait. This one hangs in his own office, where he can look at it. I've counted nine so far today.
The hangar below, and Nightglass under the test lights. From up here it looks like a hole cut in the floor.
The hangar below, the tarpaulin, and Hrubý guarding it.
A desk model of Nightglass, in gold. On the stand: "To myself, with admiration. D. V."
A black telephone with a red button marked MOSCOW and a white one marked MOTHER.
Press MOTHER? Tempting. But I have a feeling she'd recognise my voice.
December 1987. The third is ringed in red, and underneath he's written DEMONSTRATION, with three exclamation marks. Tomorrow.
Twelve medals. The Order of the Red Banner, the Hero of Karvonia, and one for Best Moustache, Karvograd Regional Finals, 1979.
Empty, except for a diary. "Dear Diary. Today I was magnificent." Every page.
A wall safe with a six-digit keypad. Vasko's safes always have six digits and always have something to do with Vasko.
Just the diary. "Dear Diary. Today I was magnificent." I'll leave it for the historians.
Six digits. Something about him, and something that matters this week. The third of December, 1987. Oh-three, twelve, eighty-seven.
Six digits. Last time it was his birthday. This time I bet it's a date too. Something he's looking forward to.
Not without the flight plans.
A flight plan. NIGHTGLASS 07, Zlatá Hora to Istanbul, tonight at midnight. Pilot: Colonel D. Vasko. He's drawn a little crown next to his name.
And a diary. "Dear Diary. Today I was magnificent." That's the whole entry. Every day.
Attention! Colonel Vasko is arriving! All personnel to the hangar! Prepare Nightglass Seven for flight!
And will somebody please catch that goose!
Time to go. Quickly, and not the way I came.
The service tunnel came out on the runway. The jet is already here, engines turning, with a ladder at the cockpit.
Search the runway! He came through the service tunnel on a tug. Nobody drives a tug that badly by accident.
Soldiers behind me, a sheer drop in front of me. And one open hatch, right there, under the belly of the aircraft.
That mechanic has a pass for the mountain. Marta will know how to handle him.
Marta gives Mirek water after his eleventh slivovitz. I could buy him a "drink".
One more "slivovitz" for Mirek, and he'll be asleep with his pass hanging out.
The bread van is waiting in the square.
The bread van in the square goes up the mountain at five.
Vlasta's boy is ill, and she has a lot of bread to carry up that mountain.
Pepík is always covered in flour, Vlasta says. Those sacks by the bakery door...
Mirek's pass would open doors inside the mountain. He's in the Golden Rooster.
Into the van, Pepík.
That woman in the white coat looks like she knows every bolt in that aircraft.
Hrubý was once bitten by a swan. My basket has something very like a swan in it.
Hrubý's gone. Dr Veselá said she'd show me what she built.
Too dark for photographs. The red switch on the lighting panel.
Lights, aircraft, camera. The Minox, on Nightglass.
The office is up the stairs. Mirek's pass should open the door.
The third of December, 1987, ringed on his calendar. Six digits.
Six digits, and it will be about Vasko. That calendar looks well used.
Out. Now.
Nothing special.
That won't work.
I don't think so.
Not a chance.
That doesn't help here.
Those two don't go together.
She's right. It steers like a pig.
Colonel?! Get out of the road!
Jack rescued Ilse's daughter from the Iron Arrow and rode a runaway mail van down the mountain to Zlatá Hora, where Madame Novak revealed she was Control's mother.
Something black flew over the valley without a sound. Colonel Vasko had not stolen the plans to build Nightglass. He had already built it.
Twelve days later. A village inn, a goose called Colonel, and a mountain that hums at night.
It is very dark, very cold and very loud. Somewhere above, a voice on the radio: "Nightglass Seven, you are cleared for take-off. Destination Istanbul."
Jack feels his way along the bay. His hand finds something warm, and feathery. Something says: honk.
Next stop: Istanbul.
Chapter Five: The Golden Horn.
Madame Novak's Minox, small enough to hide in a glove. Loaded, she says, with film that could photograph a black cat in a coal cellar.
Marta's special: a glass of water, served to anyone who has had eleven slivovitz. Nobody has ever noticed.
OBSERVATORY ZLATÁ HORA · MECHANIC · M. DVOŘÁK. The photograph has a moustache. I don't. Nobody looks at photographs.
A baker's boy's smock and cap, a little small. Pepík is twelve. I am not.
Forty rolls and one goose. The rolls are for the soldiers' supper. The goose is for emergencies.
NIGHTGLASS 07. Zlatá Hora 00:00, Istanbul 03:10, 3 December. "Demonstration for buyers." Pilot: Colonel D. Vasko. He has drawn a small crown next to his own name.
The van climbs through the pines in first gear. Forty loaves, a hundred rolls, one baker's boy, and one basket that occasionally honks.
The barrier goes up. A soldier looks in the back. "Where is Pepík?" "This is Pepík," says Vlasta. "Pepík is twelve." "He has had a very difficult year."
